about: Questions John has said the site must answer. Each one is tested by probes: multiple-choice questions a newcomer should be able to answer from the site. A probe with evidence is answered on the built site, and CI checks that it stays answered. A probe with no evidence yet is a gap the next goal audit turns into a ticket. See README.md.
not_sure: Not sure / the site doesn't say

questions.asked: how does the UK tax, debt and spending compare to other major nations
questions.reading: Major nations is read as the G7 (Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the UK and the US), with the wider OECD as context. Tax and spending are compared as a share of GDP; debt as general government gross debt as a share of GDP. Bond markets are read as government borrowing costs (10-year government bond yields) and debt interest paid as a share of GDP, compared with the G7. Yields reflect several things (central bank rates, expected inflation, how much is being borrowed and investors' view of risk), so the site should show them and explain what moves them without presenting them as a verdict on any government.

probes.question: In 2024, how did total UK tax, as a share of the economy (GDP), compare with France, Germany and Italy?

options.B: Higher than all three
options.C: Higher than Germany but lower than France and Italy
options.D: About the same as all three

probes.why: International page, 2024: UK 34.4% of GDP, against France 43.5%, Italy 42.8% and Germany 38.0%.

evidence.text: France 43.5%
Italy 42.8%
Germany 38.0%
United Kingdom 34.4%

probes.question: In 2024, how did UK government spending, as a share of GDP, compare with the United States and France?

options.B: Lower than both
options.C: Higher than the United States, lower than France
options.D: Lower than the United States, higher than France

probes.why: International page, 2024: UK 46.2% of GDP, United States 39.6%, France 57.3%.

evidence.text: United Kingdom 46.2%
United States 39.6%
France 57.3%

probes.question: How does UK government debt, as a share of GDP, compare with the other G7 countries in the latest year shown?

options.B: Higher than most of the G7, lower only than Japan
options.C: Lower than most of the G7, higher only than Germany

probes.why: Borrowing page, IMF figures for 2024: UK 101.3% of GDP, below Japan, Italy, the United States, France and Canada, above Germany (63.9%). The OECD's market-value measure gives the same order.

evidence.text: In 2024, UK government debt was 101.3% of GDP, the second lowest of the seven G7 countries: lower than Japan, Italy, the United States, France and Canada and higher than Germany.

probes.question: Where does the UK rank among the G7 countries on tax as a share of GDP, and on spending?

options.B: Lowest on both
options.C: Second lowest on tax (of the six with a figure) and fourth highest of seven on spending
options.D: Second highest on tax and lowest on spending

probes.why: International page, 2024: UK tax 34.4% of GDP, above only the United States among the six G7 countries with a figure (Japan not yet published); spending 46.2%, below France, Italy and Germany.

evidence.text: UK taxes were the second lowest as a share of GDP among the G7 (of the 6 with a figure for that year)
UK government spending was the fourth highest in 2024

probes.question: In the latest year shown, does the UK government pay more or less to borrow for 10 years than the other G7 governments?

options.A: More than every other G7 government
options.B: Less than every other G7 government
options.C: About the same as the G7 average

probes.why: Borrowing page: in 2025, the latest full year, the UK's 10-year yield averaged 4.58%, the highest of the G7; in the latest month, September 2026, it was 5.24%, also the highest.

evidence.text: In 2025, the latest full year, the market rate (yield) for new 10-year UK government borrowing averaged 4.58% a year, the highest of the G7.
The latest month, September 2026, was 5.24%, the highest of the G7.

probes.question: How does the interest the UK government pays on its debt, as a share of GDP, compare with the other G7 countries?

options.B: The third highest: below the United States and Italy
options.C: The lowest of the G7

probes.why: Borrowing page, OECD figures for 2024: UK net interest 2.2% of GDP, below the United States (4.2%) and Italy (3.6%), above France, Canada, Germany and Japan; 5.5% of revenue, also third highest.

evidence.text: In 2024, the UK government's interest payments, after subtracting interest it received, were 2.2% of GDP, the third highest of the G7: lower than the United States and Italy and higher than France, Canada, Germany and Japan.

questions.asked: Are rish people really not paying enough tax?
questions.source: John, project chat, 2026-11-04 (question 4 of his list of ten)
questions.reading: "Enough" is a value judgment, so the site gives the measured facts and does not say what is enough. The facts are: the share of Income Tax and of all taxes paid by top income groups, the share of income that each fifth of people pays in tax (including National Insurance, VAT and other taxes on spending), how the top rates compare with other countries, and what the main proposals (for example, a wealth tax or aligning Capital Gains Tax with Income Tax) are estimated to raise. Each is shown with its year, population and source.

probes.question: In tax year 2023 to 2024, what share of all Income Tax did the top 1% of Income Tax payers owe?
probes.why: Who pays page: the top 1% of Income Tax payers owed 27.2% of all Income Tax in 2023 to 2024, and had 12.4% of Income Tax payers' income. The 59.1% is the top 10%'s share of Income Tax.

evidence.text: the top 1% of Income Tax payers owed 27.2% of all Income Tax, and had 12.4% of all Income Tax payers' income

probes.question: Across 1999-00 to 2023-24, how did the top 1%'s share of Income Tax compare with their share of income?

options.A: Lower than their share of income in every year
options.B: Equal to their share of income
options.C: Higher than their share of income in every year
options.D: Higher in some years and lower in others

probes.why: Who pays page, Income Tax by person: the top 1%'s share of Income Tax was higher than their share of income in every year from 1999-00 to 2023-24.

evidence.text: The top 1%'s share of Income Tax was higher than their share of income in every year from 1999-00 to 2023-24

probes.question: What does the 46.0% figure for the richest fifth of people in 2023/24 measure?

options.A: The share of their income that they paid in tax
options.B: The share of all taxes paid by UK households that the richest fifth paid
options.C: The tax rate on the top income band
options.D: The share of all government revenue, including borrowing

probes.why: Who pays page: the richest fifth paid 46.0% of all taxes paid by UK households. The page says this is a share of the total, not the share of income that goes on tax (36.2%), and covers household taxes, not all government revenue.

evidence.text: In 2023/24 the richest fifth of people paid 46.0% of all taxes paid by UK households.
A share of the total, not the share of income that goes on tax

probes.question: In 2023/24, how did the share of gross household income that went on all taxes compare between the highest-income fifth and the lowest-income fifth?

options.A: The highest-income fifth paid a much larger share
options.B: The two shares were less than one percentage point apart
options.C: The lowest-income fifth paid a much larger share
options.D: Both paid about a quarter of their income in tax

probes.why: Tax and income page (household-tax.html): taxes took a similar share of income for the lowest-income fifth (36.7%) and the highest-income fifth (36.2%) in 2023/24, less than one percentage point apart.

evidence.text: Taxes took a similar share of income for the lowest-income fifth and the highest-income fifth in 2023/24, less than one percentage point apart

probes.question: In 2023/24, how much of the highest-income fifth's gross household income went on Income Tax alone?
probes.why: Tax and income page: for people in the highest-income fifth most tax is direct, and Income Tax alone was 22.3% of gross household income. The 36.2% is all taxes for that fifth.

evidence.text: Income Tax alone was 22.3% of gross household income

probes.question: According to the site, how much would the main proposals to tax wealth or capital gains more heavily raise each year?
probes.gap: The site does not yet show what Capital Gains Tax and Inheritance Tax raise, or estimate what wealth tax or Capital Gains Tax changes would raise.

probes.question: According to the site, how do the UK's rates on top incomes compare with other large countries?
probes.gap: The international page compares total tax as a share of GDP, but does not compare top income tax rates or the tax paid by top earners with other countries.

probes.question: According to the site, what share of all taxes, including VAT and National Insurance, do the top 1% of people pay?
probes.gap: The site shows the top 1%'s share of Income Tax only, not their share of all taxes, so the top 1%'s total tax share is not shown.

questions.asked: Is immigration a good thing or a bad thing?
questions.reading: The site does not say whether immigration is good or bad. That is a judgment that depends on values. It answers what official evidence says about the parts that can be measured: the public-money effects of migrants by type, use of public services, the NHS and care workforce, and population and growth. It says which parts are evidence and which depend on values, and shows the range of credible estimates. Immigration is read as people moving to live in the UK (net migration, all routes), with EU and non-EU migrants shown separately where official figures split them. The answer should be easy to find from the home page in a few taps on a phone.

probes.question: Does the site say whether immigration is a good thing or a bad thing?
probes.gap: There is no immigration page yet. It must say plainly that good or bad depends on values, that it does not decide that, and which parts the evidence does settle, reachable in a few taps from the home page.

probes.question: According to official estimates, does a migrant's effect on public finances depend on their age, visa route or employment?
probes.gap: No page shows fiscal effects of migrants yet. It must show the OBR and Migration Advisory Committee estimates by migrant type (age, visa route, employment), with the period, population and units.

probes.question: Do official estimates of migrants' effect on public finances differ between the short run and the long run?
probes.gap: The site must show whether the official estimates give different results over short and long periods, with the period and main assumptions for each.

probes.question: Does the site show how much migrants use public services such as the NHS, schools and housing, using official figures?
probes.gap: No public-services use page yet. It must show what official sources measure about migrants' use of public services and say where they cannot separate migrants from other people.

probes.question: In the latest official figures, what share of NHS and adult social care staff in England are non-UK nationals?
probes.gap: No workforce page yet. It must show the latest NHS England and Skills for Care figures on non-UK nationals in the NHS and adult social care, with the date and definition used.

probes.question: In the latest ONS population figures, what was the main reason the UK population grew?
probes.gap: The population page shows total population only. It must show ONS net migration and natural change for the latest year, with the year and the source.

probes.question: According to official economic estimates, does migration raise GDP per person as much as it raises total GDP?
probes.gap: No economic-effects page yet. It must show what the OBR and other official estimates say about migration's effect on total GDP and on GDP per person, and explain the difference.

probes.question: Where official sources give different estimates of the same thing, does the site show the range rather than one chosen figure?
probes.gap: Each immigration estimate must show the range from the official sources, with no single figure picked to favour a view. Nothing on the site does this for immigration yet.

questions.asked: What are the empirical best ways to get the UK economy into a better position, a ranked list of ten things
questions.reading: Ten options, ranked only by a stated, published, empirical measure, never by the site's opinion. The measure is the size of a published estimate of the effect on the level of GDP (potential GDP) over a stated horizon, shown with its range, cost and uncertainty. Estimates from different sources or models are not like-for-like, so they must not be ranked against each other as if they were; where only one source covers a set of options, the ranking stays inside that set. 'Better position' depends on goals (growth, fairness, the deficit), so the site should say that a second ranking, by cost to the public finances, may differ.

probes.question: According to the OECD's modelling of UK structural reforms, which reform package raises the level of GDP most within ten years?

options.A: Trade barriers and research and development support
options.B: Getting people on long-term sick leave back into work
options.C: Planning reform, full expensing and access to finance
options.D: Keeping the state pension triple lock

probes.why: The OECD estimates planning reform, full expensing and access to finance at +2.1% of potential GDP after 10 years, the largest of its packages (long-term sick +1.4%, trade and R&D +0.5%).

evidence.text: Capital deepening: planning reform, extension of full expensing, access to finance

probes.question: What does the OECD estimate the full combined UK reform package would raise the level of potential GDP by, after ten years and after 25 years?

options.B: +4.0% after 10 years and +7.7% after 25 years
options.C: +0.5% after 10 years and +1.7% after 25 years

probes.why: The OECD's combined package is +4.0% of potential GDP after 10 years and +7.7% after 25 years.

evidence.text: gives +4.0% of potential GDP after 10 years and +7.7% after 25 years

probes.question: What measure do the OECD's reform estimates use for the size of each effect?

options.B: A percentage of baseline potential GDP
options.C: Change in employment numbers

probes.why: The OECD measures each effect as a percentage of baseline potential GDP.

evidence.text: a percentage of baseline potential GDP

questions.asked: Are people really leaving the UK becasue taxes are too high and living standards are too low?
questions.reading: Read as two questions. First: are more people leaving the UK than before? Official figures can answer this for emigration overall and for British, EU+ and non-EU+ nationals, and for non-domiciled taxpayers at HMRC. Second: are taxes or living standards the reason? No official source records why people leave, so the site can only say what the figures can and cannot show about that.

probes.question: About how many people left the UK to live abroad for at least 12 months in the year ending December 2025 (provisional)?

options.B: About 642,000
options.C: About 278,000

probes.why: ONS gives 642,000 for total long-term emigration in the year ending December 2025. The 246,000 figure is British nationals only.

evidence.text: The provisional estimate for total long-term emigration in the most recent period is 642,000.

probes.question: How did the number of British nationals leaving the UK change from the year ending December 2024 to the year ending December 2025?

options.B: It fell slightly, from 257,000 to 246,000
options.C: It stayed exactly the same

probes.why: ONS: 246,000 British nationals left in the year ending December 2025, a 4% decline from the updated figure of 257,000 for 2024.

evidence.text: In YE December 2025, 246,000 British nationals left the UK, a slight decline of 4% from the updated YE December 2024 estimates of 257,000.

probes.question: Do the official figures show why people leave the UK?

options.A: Yes, they record the main reason each person gave
options.B: Yes, but only for people who leave for work
options.C: No, they record when people leave, not why

probes.why: The ONS records the visa or route a person first arrived on, not a reason for leaving. No official figure here records why anyone left.

evidence.text: None of the official figures on this page records why anyone left.

probes.question: Can the British emigration figures for 2025 be compared with those before June 2021?

options.A: Yes, the method has not changed
options.B: No, the way British departures are estimated changed, so they cannot be compared
options.C: Yes, both show record levels

probes.why: ONS changed its method for British nationals and revised the series back to June 2021, but says earlier figures cannot be compared with the new ones.

evidence.text: The significant change in our methods means we cannot compare our improved estimates with those from before June 2021.

probes.question: What happened to the number of non-domiciled taxpayers leaving that group in the tax year 2024 to 2025 (HMRC)?

options.B: It fell to about 9,000, from about 11,200
options.C: It stayed at about 11,200

probes.why: HMRC: around 9,000 taxpayers flowed out of the non-domiciled group in 2024 to 2025, compared with 11,200 the year before.

evidence.text: Fewer taxpayers flowed out of the non-domiciled taxpayer population than in the previous year (around 9,000 compared with 11,200), while the number of newly arrived non-domiciled taxpayers also fell (around 8,600 compared with 10,000).

probes.question: What happened to the Income Tax paid by non-domiciled and deemed domiciled taxpayers in the tax year 2024 to 2025 (HMRC)?

options.B: It rose by 6%, to its highest level since 2017
options.C: It stayed the same

probes.why: HMRC: Income Tax from this group was £556 million (6%) higher than the year before, at its highest level since 2017.

evidence.text: At around £9.7 billion, the Income Tax revenue from non-domiciled and deemed domiciled taxpayers is £556 million (or 6%) higher than in tax year ending 2024 and is at its highest level since tax year ending 2017.

probes.question: Can these official figures show whether taxes or living standards were a reason people left?

options.B: Yes, but only for high earners
options.C: No, the figures on this page cannot show it
options.D: Yes, the tax figures show it directly

probes.why: None of the sources here records why people left, what they paid in tax, or how their living standards changed. The site says so and points to separate pages.

evidence.text: The figures on this page cannot show whether taxes or living standards were a reason for leaving.

probes.question: How many more British nationals left the UK than arrived in 2025, on ONS's provisional figures?

options.B: About 136,000
options.C: About 246,000

probes.why: ONS: around 136,000 more British nationals left than arrived in 2025. The 110,000 figure is British arrivals.

evidence.text: Around 136,000 more Brits left than arrived in 2025.
